newsitem.title: UK: Labour minister seeks radical UK welfare shakeup.
newsitem.headline: Labour minister seeks radical UK welfare shakeup.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government must radically overhaul the welfare state if it is to avoid serious damage to the public finances, social security minister Frank Field warned on Sunday.

Field, appointed by Prime Minister Tony Blair as minister of state for social security on Saturday, wrote in the Sunday Telegraph newspaper that sweeping reforms were needed to bring Britain's welfare bill under control.
"Bold new initiatives are now needed if welfare expenditure is not to derail the new government's financial probity," Field said. He wrote the article before being made a minister.
Welfare reform is crucial if Labour's pledge to meet the Conservatives' tight public spending plans over the next two years is to be achieved.
Outgoing Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Sunday that his successor, Gordon Brown, had little or no chance of keeping the lid on spending.

Field said annual welfare spending was about to break the 100 billion pounds barrier. The Conservative approach had been to tighten up rules over eligibility -- "arming more effectively the gatekeepers to welfare's eligibility," as he put it.
That option had been fully explored and yet the welfare budget had kept on rising.
"Labour will need to embrace radical reform if this budget it to be kept under control," he said.
Field has developed a reputation as one of Britain's foremost thinkers on welfare reform during his time as chairman of parliament's Social Security Select Committee.
His ministerial role will put him at the head of long-term planning for welfare reform. Downing Street aides said Blair had "immense respect" for him.

Field said the pension system needed overhauling first but the Conservatives' proposed "Basic Pensions Plus" plan, under which national insurance payments would be given to private sector funds to invest on an individual's behalf, was not the way forward.
During the election campaign, Labour accused the Conservatives of planning to abolish the state pension, a charge which the former government vigorously denied.

"I believe the state pension needs to be kept as the first tier of common pension provision," Field said. "The task of the new parliament will be to universalise second-funded pension provision," to take the pressure off public finances.
Economists warn of a "demographic timebomb" to describe the situation in which a growing number of old people has to be supported by the taxes of an ever-dwindling workforce.
Field said Britons wanted low, American-style tax rates and high, European-style welfare benefits but this was an impossibility.
He said reforms aimed directly at cutting welfare spending were needed and single-parent families were a key section of society to tackle.
He suggested a private finance scheme for university student grants, which would have to be paid back through a graduate tax.
This could raise 1.2 billion pounds to be spent on child care and nursery education, prompting "vast numbers of single mothers to seek work," Field said.
"The norm would then become one where single mothers worked, which is what most want to do anyway."
Field's new boss, Social Security Secretary Harriet Harman, backed his call for help for single mothers.
"Lone mothers often face huge problems moving off benefit and into work. But it is a step the vast majority of them want to make," she told London Weekend Television.
"I shall be starting with the biggest barrier they have to cross, namely access to childcare. I shall start talking to the key groups involved in this area within the next few days."
